facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The financial base is usable for a credit snapshot of the consolidated Partnership, with limitations. Reported statements for FY2025, the first nine months of 2026 and Q3 2026 are complete and internally consistent (the quarterly Adjusted EBITDA figures sum to the nine-month figure; see Calculations). Scale changed sharply because Parkland was acquired on 2025-10-31, so FY2025 contains two months of Parkland and the trailing Q3 2026 window contains eleven. The FY2025 leverage ratios are therefore overstated relative to a pro forma view, and the trailing Q3 2026 ratios are modestly overstated too. The management-reported covenant net leverage (4.03x at FY2025, 3.98x, 3.7x and 3.5x through Q3 2026) tracks the derived net ratio closely only at Q3 2026, which is consistent with the covenant definition being pro forma for acquisitions and netting reserved cash. Debt is dominated by unsecured senior notes with guarantees from subsidiaries; liquidity rests on a single 2,500 US$m revolver maturing 2030-06-17. Earnings quality needs care: Adjusted EBITDA adds back equity-affiliate EBITDA and a large non-cash adjustment, and excludes a favourable inventory valuation adjustment. None of these restricts the base, but each is carried into later modules.

facts.label: Debt and claims outside debt
facts.text: Debt at 2026-09-30 is 13,163 US$m (carrying), made up of senior notes, the revolver, GoZone bonds, lease-related financing and other subsidiary debt, less 80 US$m of issuance costs (Q3 10-Q page:13). Issuers and guarantors, as the filing states: notes of Sunoco LP and Sunoco Finance Corp. (co-issuer) are guaranteed by NuStar Logistics and other subsidiaries; notes of NuStar Logistics are guaranteed by Sunoco LP, Sunoco Finance Corp. and subsidiaries; guarantees rank equally with other unsecured senior debt of each guarantor and are structurally subordinated to debt of non-guarantor subsidiaries (Q3 10-Q page:46 and page:47). The 10-K says the Sunoco senior notes are effectively subordinated to the issuers' and guarantors' secured obligations, including the Credit Facility, to the extent of the collateral value (10-K page:250), and that the Credit Facility is guaranteed by material domestic subsidiaries (10-K page:251); the collateral package is not described in the sources. Energy Transfer guarantees collection of the principal of the 5.875% senior notes due 2028 (10-K page:250). During 2026 the Partnership issued 600 US$m of 5.375% notes due 2031 and 600 US$m of 5.625% notes due 2034 and redeemed the 6.000% notes due 2026 and 2027, the Parkland notes not exchanged, the 3.875% CAD notes due 2026 and the 6.000% CAD notes due 2028 (Q3 10-Q page:14). Notes repaid in the nine months were 1,878 US$m against 1,200 US$m borrowed (Q3 10-Q page:5 and page:6).

facts.label: Definition review
facts.text: Adjusted EBITDA is the Partnership's non-GAAP measure and "is used as a performance measure under our Credit Facility" (Q3 10-Q page:32). It starts at net income and adds back interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation and accretion, unit-based compensation, disposal losses and impairments, extinguishment losses, unrealised commodity derivative effects, inventory valuation adjustments, certain foreign exchange effects and other items; it adds Adjusted EBITDA of unconsolidated affiliates and subtracts their equity earnings (Q3 10-Q page:21 and page:22). For the nine months of 2026 the add-back for unconsolidated affiliates is 200 US$m, other non-cash adjustments are 131 US$m, and the inventory valuation adjustment removes 445 US$m of favourable effect (Q3 10-Q page:33). The Q3 release headline of 1.060 billion US$ excludes one-time transaction-related expenses of 11 US$m, whereas the filing and the release body show 1,049 US$m (release Q3 page:2). This handoff uses the filing figure. Differences from the covenant ratio: the covenant net leverage uses the credit-agreement Net Leverage Ratio, which after a 2025 amendment provided for up to 2.00 billion US$ of cash reserved for the Parkland consideration to be netted (10-K page:252) and is not computed from statements here.

facts.label: Cash flow and earnings quality
facts.text: Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow was 2,251 US$m on net income of 1,426 US$m, with working capital contributing a 316 US$m inflow (the cash flow effect of accounts receivable was an outflow of 2,313 US$m and that of accounts payable an inflow of 1,479 US$m, Q3 10-Q page:11). The inventory valuation adjustment of 445 US$m raised net income without cash and is reversed in cash flow. A last-in first-out liquidation in the first quarter raised pre-tax income by 102 US$m (Q3 10-Q page:12). A foreign exchange loss of 94 US$m was non-cash (Q3 10-Q page:42). Acquisitions in the nine months were TanQuid (194 US$m net of cash), Delta (75 US$m) and other (87 US$m) (Q3 10-Q page:5). Distributions of 880 US$m were paid in the nine months, including 151 US$m to the Class D unitholder and 118 US$m to preferred unitholders (Q3 10-Q page:6). The distribution declared for Q3 2026 is 1.0148 US$ per common unit, payable 2026-11-19, about 139 US$m on common units, 52 US$m on Class D units and 76 US$m to incentive distribution rights (Q3 10-Q page:44). Segment Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026 was Fuel Distribution 523, Pipeline Systems 166, Terminals 122 and Refinery 238 US$m (Q3 10-Q page:22); the Refinery segment sells largely to other segments (intersegment revenues 853 US$m of 970 US$m in the quarter, page:22).

Liquidity is 3,060 US$m: cash of 760 US$m plus 2,300 US$m of undrawn revolver, after 111 US$m drawn and 84 US$m of letters of credit.
Trailing Adjusted EBITDA rose to 3,535 US$m from 2,047 US$m in FY2025, with Q3 2026 alone at 1,049 US$m.
Reported covenant net leverage is 3.5x at Q3 2026; the FY2025 filing sets a 5.50x ceiling and a 2.25x minimum interest cover.
Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow of 2,251 US$m exceeded capital expenditure of 579 US$m; distributions paid were 880 US$m and working capital added 316 US$m.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: The business is a four-segment energy infrastructure and fuel distribution group: Fuel Distribution, Pipeline Systems, Terminals and Refinery. It operates across 33 countries and territories in North America, the Greater Caribbean and Europe, with about 14,000 miles of pipeline, over 170 terminals and capacity to distribute over 17 billion gallons annually (Q3 10-Q page:7). The step change came from the Parkland acquisition on 2025-10-31, which added Canadian and Caribbean distribution and the Burnaby refinery, on top of the NuStar acquisition of 2024-05-03, which added pipelines and terminals. Ownership is concentrated: Energy Transfer owns the general partner, a minority of the common units and all incentive distribution rights, and through SunocoCorp controls the board appointment right. The creditor view is a larger, more diversified earnings base than before the acquisitions, financed largely with debt and preferred equity, under a sponsor whose economic interest (incentive distributions) is separate from that of the debt holders. Documented behaviour since 2024 shows continued acquisition activity paired with reported leverage reduction and rising distributions, which is mixed for creditors rather than adverse. The decisive open items are the fair-value work on Parkland, TanQuid, Delta and Offen, the funding of Offen, and the absence of the executed documents that set distribution, debt and change-of-control limits.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The defining transaction is the Parkland acquisition, completed on 2025-10-31 by Sunoco Retail LLC, a wholly owned corporate subsidiary. Parkland shareholders received 0.295 SunocoCorp units and C$19.80 in cash per Parkland share, or could elect cash or units subject to proration. The Partnership paid about 2.60 billion US$ to Parkland shareholders and transferred 51,517,198 SunocoCorp common units, which it had received in exchange for issuing 51,517,198 Class D Units to SunocoCorp (10-K page:7). Total consideration was 5,015 US$m (4,551 US$m net of cash acquired), against assumed long-term debt of 3,797 US$m, goodwill of 1,528 US$m and intangible assets of 1,871 US$m, all on a preliminary allocation (10-K page:238). The cash portion was funded in part by the September 2025 issuance of 1.00 billion US$ of 5.625% senior notes due 2031 and 900 million US$ of 5.875% senior notes due 2034, and by the 1.5 million Series A Preferred Units sold for net proceeds of about 1.47 billion US$ (10-K page:140). The Parkland senior note exchange closed on 2025-11-07 with about C$1.47 billion and 2.58 billion US$ of Parkland notes tendered, leaving 111 US$m of Parkland notes outstanding at 2025-12-31 (10-K page:140 and page:139); the Q3 10-Q shows those residual Parkland notes redeemed in 2026 (page:14). SunocoCorp was repurposed as a publicly traded corporation holding the Class D Units, and the Partnership must keep SunocoCorp distributions equal to its own through the equalisation period (Q3 10-Q page:19).

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: In 2026 the Partnership acquired TanQuid on 2026-01-16 (15 fuel terminals in Germany and one in Poland) for 239 US$m with 346 US$m of assumed debt at fair value, funded from cash and the revolving credit facility, and Delta on 2026-04-01 for about 81 US$m, with terminals and distribution assets in five Caribbean markets (Q3 10-Q page:9 and page:10). Purchase accounting for TanQuid is preliminary. After quarter end, on 2026-10-27, Sunoco Retail acquired Offen Petroleum, a US fuel distributor of about 2.5 billion gallons a year, for about 600 US$m in cash plus working capital; the funding source and the effect on 2026-10-31 liquidity are not stated, and fair value work is incomplete (Q3 10-Q page:10). On 2026-10-08 the receivables financing agreement was terminated with no borrowings outstanding (Q3 10-Q page:15).

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: New debt issued in the period: in March 2025, 1.00 billion US$ of 6.250% senior notes due 2033, used to repay 600 US$m of 5.750% notes due 2025 and part of the revolver (10-K page:140); in September 2025, the 5.625% 2031 and 5.875% 2034 notes above; in March 2026, 600 US$m of 5.375% senior notes due 2031 and 600 US$m of 5.625% senior notes due 2034, both maturing on 2031-07-15 and 2034-07-15, with part of the proceeds used to redeem the 500 US$m 6.000% notes due 2026 and the 600 US$m 6.000% notes due 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:14). Net of these redemptions the March 2026 issuance added 100 US$m of principal. Parkland's remaining notes were redeemed in March 2026, the 3.875% CAD notes due 2026 in June 2026 and the 6.000% CAD notes due 2028 in August 2026. The earlier history includes the NuStar acquisition of 2024-05-03 (about 51.5 million Sunoco common units issued, about 3.5 billion US$ of debt assumed, and NuStar preferred units, subordinated notes and credit facility repaid after closing), the sale of 204 West Texas convenience stores to 7-Eleven on 2024-04-16 for about 1.0 billion US$ with a 586 US$m gain, and the formation of the ET-S Permian joint venture with Energy Transfer on 2024-07-01 (10-K page:240 to page:242).

facts.label: Ownership, governance and sponsor behaviour
facts.text: Energy Transfer owns 100% of the general partner membership interest, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights, and controls SunocoCorp, which owns all Class D Units (Q3 10-Q page:7). Under a Delegation Agreement dated 2025-10-27, Energy Transfer delegated its power to elect, appoint and remove the Sunoco GP LLC board to SunocoCorp; the rights terminate on certain SunocoCorp insolvency events or at Energy Transfer's election, and the general partner agreed not to amend the partnership agreement against those rights or to withdraw while SunocoCorp is listed or not wholly owned by Energy Transfer (10-K page:197). The 10-K states that general partner officers and directors "also have a contractual duty to manage our General Partner in a manner beneficial to Energy Transfer" and that conflicts of interest may arise (10-K page:91). An Omnibus Agreement dated 2025-10-31 has the Partnership indemnify SunocoCorp, provide all general and administrative services and fund SunocoCorp's distributions equal to those on Sunoco common units through the eighth full quarter after closing (10-K page:197 and page:198).

facts.text: Evidence: Four acquisitions closed in twelve months with open fair value work (10-K page:238; Q3 10-Q page:9 and page:10). facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Sunoco LP is a sponsor-controlled fuel distribution and midstream credit whose leverage has fallen to about 3.5x and whose liquidity is ample. Its strongest support is scale and diversification: trailing Adjusted EBITDA of USD 3,535 million across four segments, net debt of 3.51x that figure, and liquidity of USD 3,060 million against USD 1,049 million of notes due in 2027. The weakest point is that the improvement rests on recently acquired earnings, management-adjusted EBITDA and a sponsor whose incentive distributions and board control sit beside creditor interests, while funding for the USD 600 million Offen purchase is not described. Whether Parkland integration and refinery margins keep earnings at this level decides whether leverage keeps falling.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Leverage has fallen sharply, but part of the fall is perimeter change. Sunoco LP's net debt over trailing Adjusted EBITDA fell from 6.11x at FY2025 to 3.51x at Q3 2026, and the reported covenant net leverage fell from 4.03x to 3.5x [CP-1]. The mechanism is that Parkland (acquired on 2025-10-31) contributed two months to FY2025 earnings but eleven months to the Q3 2026 trailing window while its debt was fully on the balance sheet at both dates [CP-1, CP-1A]. The implication is that headroom against the 5.50x covenant ceiling is wide on the reported basis, yet the trajectory should be judged on pro forma earnings that the sources do not supply.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Liquidity is strong against a staggered maturity profile. Sunoco LP held USD 760 million of cash and USD 2,300 million of undrawn revolver, total USD 3,060 million, at 2026-09-30, after USD 111 million drawn and USD 84 million of letters of credit [CP-1]. Maturities are USD 1,049 million in 2027, USD 900 million in 2028, USD 2,723 million in 2029 and USD 2,309 million in 2030 including the revolver [CP-1]. The 2027 notes are classified as long-term only on management's intent and ability to refinance, so the mechanism is market access rather than cash on hand. The implication is that refinancing risk is low in the next twelve months and moderate in 2027 to 2029, when USD 4,672 million falls due.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Cash generation covers distributions, with timing help. Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow of USD 2,251 million exceeded capital expenditure of USD 579 million and distributions of USD 880 million [CP-1]. The mechanism includes a USD 316 million working-capital inflow, a USD 102 million last-in first-out liquidation benefit to pre-tax income and a USD 94 million non-cash foreign exchange loss [CP-1]. The implication is that free cash flow after distributions is positive (see Calculations) but is not a stable annuity: it depends on working capital timing and fuel prices.

Adjusted EBITDA is a management measure that adds back USD 200 million of unconsolidated affiliate EBITDA, USD 131 million of other non-cash adjustments and removes a USD 445 million favourable inventory valuation adjustment in nine months 2026 [CP-1]. Covenant ratios use credit-agreement definitions that are not supplied [CP-0, CP-1]. The implication is that the derived ratios in this synthesis are a guide and the covenant headroom is a reported claim, not a verified result.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Structure and control weigh on creditor protection. Energy Transfer owns the general partner, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights, and controls the board appointment right through SunocoCorp [CP-1A]. Notes are guaranteed by subsidiaries and rank effectively behind secured obligations including the revolver, and structurally behind debt of non-guarantor subsidiaries, which hold USD 11.73 billion of long-term assets (Q3 10-Q page:47); the line for lease-related financing and other subsidiary debt is USD 597 million and its obligors are not identified [CP-1]. The implication is that the capacity to pay out cash or add debt depends on indenture and partnership agreement terms that are not supplied, so legal capacity is not assessed.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Acquisition pace is the main forward risk. Four acquisitions closed within twelve months, the latest being Offen on 2026-10-27 for about USD 600 million in cash [CP-1A]. The mechanism is that purchase prices and acquired debt enter the balance sheet at once while earnings arrive gradually, and fair value work is open. An all-debt illustration would lift net leverage to about 3.68x before any Offen earnings (see Calculations). The implication is that further leverage movement depends on funding choice and integration.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. Scale and diversification (Documentary Fact): four segments with Fuel Distribution, Pipeline Systems, Terminals and Refinery all contributing in Q3 2026, and operations in 33 countries and territories [CP-1A]. This reduces dependence on one margin source and supports revenue visibility. Fee-based and contracted income (Documentary Fact): pipeline and terminal throughput, remaining performance obligations of USD 2,038 million and a 15-year take-or-pay fuel supply agreement with minimum gross profit with the largest customer [CP-1A]. This supports cash conversion in weaker fuel-margin periods. Liquidity and maturity management (Documentary Fact): USD 3,060 million of liquidity, a revolver maturing 2030-06-17 and 2026 and 2027 notes replaced by notes due 2031 and 2034 [CP-1, CP-1A]. This lowers near-term refinancing risk. Deleveraging record (Documentary Fact): covenant net leverage reported at 4.03x, 3.98x, 3.7x and 3.5x across the last four reporting dates [CP-1]. This shows a funding and earnings path that creditors can monitor. Equity cushion (Analyst Interpretation): total equity of USD 8,512 million including USD 1,477 million of preferred units sits beneath USD 13,163 million of debt, which is 60.7% of debt plus equity (see Calculations) [CP-1]. Preferred and Class D equity were used for part of the Parkland price [CP-1A].

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Weaknesses. Acquisition dependence (Documentary Fact): Parkland, TanQuid, Delta and Offen in twelve months with open fair value work [CP-1A]. This makes trailing metrics unrepresentative and exposes leverage to integration. Sponsor control and cash leakage (Documentary Fact): Energy Transfer control, incentive distributions at the top tier share and a general partner that must favour Energy Transfer's interests under its contractual duty [CP-1A]. This competes with debt reduction for cash. Commodity and single-site exposure (Analyst Interpretation): the Burnaby Refinery earned USD 238 million of Segment Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026, largely on intersegment sales whose pricing terms are not described [CP-1A]. This adds margin volatility. Thin per-gallon margins and working capital swings (Analyst Interpretation): fuel is most of revenue and working capital moved by USD 316 million in nine months 2026 [CP-1, CP-1A]. Customer concentration (Documentary Fact): 7-Eleven was about 13% of FY2025 revenues [CP-1A]. Disclosure limits (Insufficient Information): the indentures, credit agreement, partnership agreement, ratings and pro forma earnings are not supplied, which stops conclusions on covenant headroom, restricted payments and rating-linked pricing. Market view of the debt (Documentary Fact): the aggregate fair value of debt was USD 12.88 billion against a carrying amount of USD 13.16 billion at 2026-09-30, the reverse of the position at 2025-12-31 (Q3 10-Q page:15); the sources do not explain the move.

### Financial base view

The financial base is usable for a credit snapshot of the consolidated Partnership, with limitations. Reported statements for FY2025, the first nine months of 2026 and Q3 2026 are complete and internally consistent (the quarterly Adjusted EBITDA figures sum to the nine-month figure; see Calculations). Scale changed sharply because Parkland was acquired on 2025-10-31, so FY2025 contains two months of Parkland and the trailing Q3 2026 window contains eleven. The FY2025 leverage ratios are therefore overstated relative to a pro forma view, and the trailing Q3 2026 ratios are modestly overstated too. The management-reported covenant net leverage (4.03x at FY2025, 3.98x, 3.7x and 3.5x through Q3 2026) tracks the derived net ratio closely only at Q3 2026, which is consistent with the covenant definition being pro forma for acquisitions and netting reserved cash. Debt is dominated by unsecured senior notes with guarantees from subsidiaries; liquidity rests on a single 2,500 US$m revolver maturing 2030-06-17. Earnings quality needs care: Adjusted EBITDA adds back equity-affiliate EBITDA and a large non-cash adjustment, and excludes a favourable inventory valuation adjustment. None of these restricts the base, but each is carried into later modules.

### Debt and claims outside debt

Debt at 2026-09-30 is 13,163 US$m (carrying), made up of senior notes, the revolver, GoZone bonds, lease-related financing and other subsidiary debt, less 80 US$m of issuance costs (Q3 10-Q page:13). Issuers and guarantors, as the filing states: notes of Sunoco LP and Sunoco Finance Corp. (co-issuer) are guaranteed by NuStar Logistics and other subsidiaries; notes of NuStar Logistics are guaranteed by Sunoco LP, Sunoco Finance Corp. and subsidiaries; guarantees rank equally with other unsecured senior debt of each guarantor and are structurally subordinated to debt of non-guarantor subsidiaries (Q3 10-Q page:46 and page:47). The 10-K says the Sunoco senior notes are effectively subordinated to the issuers' and guarantors' secured obligations, including the Credit Facility, to the extent of the collateral value (10-K page:250), and that the Credit Facility is guaranteed by material domestic subsidiaries (10-K page:251); the collateral package is not described in the sources. Energy Transfer guarantees collection of the principal of the 5.875% senior notes due 2028 (10-K page:250). During 2026 the Partnership issued 600 US$m of 5.375% notes due 2031 and 600 US$m of 5.625% notes due 2034 and redeemed the 6.000% notes due 2026 and 2027, the Parkland notes not exchanged, the 3.875% CAD notes due 2026 and the 6.000% CAD notes due 2028 (Q3 10-Q page:14). Notes repaid in the nine months were 1,878 US$m against 1,200 US$m borrowed (Q3 10-Q page:5 and page:6).

Claims outside the debt figure: operating lease liabilities of 185 US$m current and 1,375 US$m non-current (Q3 10-Q page:3); Series A Preferred Units of 1,477 US$m at a 7.875% rate with 39.375 US$ per unit paid semi-annually, which are equity and not debt (Q3 10-Q page:3 and page:20); Class D units held by SunocoCorp with distribution equalisation through 2027-12-31 (Q3 10-Q page:19); environmental liabilities of 213 US$m and asset retirement obligations of 214 US$m (Q3 10-Q page:18 and page:15 to page:16); a New York motor fuel excise tax assessment of about 20 US$m under appeal (Q3 10-Q page:18). The pension plan was terminated in 2024 and the benefit obligation was nil at 2025-12-31 (10-K page:274). Purchase commitments, factoring and supply-chain finance were searched in the 10-K and the Q3 10-Q and no such disclosure was found. Debt-like lease financing obligations are inside the 597 US$m line.

Covenants: the 10-K states a maximum Net Leverage Ratio of 5.50 to 1.00 before an investment grade rating and a minimum Interest Coverage Ratio of 2.25 to 1.00 (10-K page:251). The Q3 10-Q reports net leverage of 3.5 to 1.00 and compliance with all financial covenants (page:15). The reported interest coverage ratio is not printed in any source. The step-down to 5.00 to 1.00 applies only after an investment grade rating, and no rating is supplied.
### Definition review

Adjusted EBITDA is the Partnership's non-GAAP measure and "is used as a performance measure under our Credit Facility" (Q3 10-Q page:32). It starts at net income and adds back interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation and accretion, unit-based compensation, disposal losses and impairments, extinguishment losses, unrealised commodity derivative effects, inventory valuation adjustments, certain foreign exchange effects and other items; it adds Adjusted EBITDA of unconsolidated affiliates and subtracts their equity earnings (Q3 10-Q page:21 and page:22). For the nine months of 2026 the add-back for unconsolidated affiliates is 200 US$m, other non-cash adjustments are 131 US$m, and the inventory valuation adjustment removes 445 US$m of favourable effect (Q3 10-Q page:33). The Q3 release headline of 1.060 billion US$ excludes one-time transaction-related expenses of 11 US$m, whereas the filing and the release body show 1,049 US$m (release Q3 page:2). This handoff uses the filing figure. Differences from the covenant ratio: the covenant net leverage uses the credit-agreement Net Leverage Ratio, which after a 2025 amendment provided for up to 2.00 billion US$ of cash reserved for the Parkland consideration to be netted (10-K page:252) and is not computed from statements here.
### Cash flow and earnings quality

Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow was 2,251 US$m on net income of 1,426 US$m, with working capital contributing a 316 US$m inflow (the cash flow effect of accounts receivable was an outflow of 2,313 US$m and that of accounts payable an inflow of 1,479 US$m, Q3 10-Q page:11). The inventory valuation adjustment of 445 US$m raised net income without cash and is reversed in cash flow. A last-in first-out liquidation in the first quarter raised pre-tax income by 102 US$m (Q3 10-Q page:12). A foreign exchange loss of 94 US$m was non-cash (Q3 10-Q page:42). Acquisitions in the nine months were TanQuid (194 US$m net of cash), Delta (75 US$m) and other (87 US$m) (Q3 10-Q page:5). Distributions of 880 US$m were paid in the nine months, including 151 US$m to the Class D unitholder and 118 US$m to preferred unitholders (Q3 10-Q page:6). The distribution declared for Q3 2026 is 1.0148 US$ per common unit, payable 2026-11-19, about 139 US$m on common units, 52 US$m on Class D units and 76 US$m to incentive distribution rights (Q3 10-Q page:44). Segment Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026 was Fuel Distribution 523, Pipeline Systems 166, Terminals 122 and Refinery 238 US$m (Q3 10-Q page:22); the Refinery segment sells largely to other segments (intersegment revenues 853 US$m of 970 US$m in the quarter, page:22).
### Latest quarter and subsequent events

On 2026-10-27, after the balance sheet date, Sunoco Retail acquired Offen Petroleum for about 600 US$m in cash plus working capital; fair value work is incomplete (Q3 10-Q page:10). On 2026-10-08 the receivables financing agreement was terminated with no borrowings outstanding (page:15). On 2026-10-22 the Q3 distribution was announced (page:44). The Q3 release says the Partnership expects to exceed its 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance of 3.5 billion to 3.7 billion US$ (release Q3 page:2); this is a management claim. In the first nine months the Partnership also completed the TanQuid acquisition (2026-01-16, 239 US$m purchase price and 346 US$m of assumed debt at fair value) and the Delta acquisition (2026-04-01, about 81 US$m) (Q3 10-Q page:9 and page:10). The funding source for Offen is not stated in the sources.
## Calculations
All inputs are US$m from the cited pages. LTM = FY2025 + current year-to-date − prior year-to-date.
| Calculation | Formula and inputs | Result |

spans.text: ## Request

Module CP-1A (business and transaction context) for Sunoco LP (ticker SUN), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot, reporting currency USD, current period Q3 2026, prior period FY2025. The question is which transaction, ownership, business, operating and governance facts matter most to a creditor of the consolidated Partnership. The entity is Sunoco LP and its consolidated subsidiaries; the general partner is Sunoco GP LLC. Nothing dated after the 2026-11-05 cutoff is used. Events after 2026-09-30 are labelled subsequent events. Figures are US$ millions (US$m) unless stated and are taken from the accepted financial-base handoff or from the cited page. No peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion is given.
## Sources
### Issuer sources relied on
| Source file (exact name) | sha256 |
| EX-99.1_2026-11-03_ex991sunocoandsunococorper.htm.jsonl | 9cda190739e5a6207ea6c7ec1f929f6d3b9334edb87da0e79d1dca3af0892d56 |

Citations read file and page, for example "Q3 10-Q page:10" is the Q3 2026 10-Q source chunk page:10 and "10-K page:7" is the FY2025 10-K chunk page:7. The releases are management language and are tagged so below.
### Handoffs relied on
| Module | sha256 |
| CP-0 | 57b161fbd7e67eac0d6f2f2ef29f60aa3fbd5113ce9bed40f825ee33e1b2f40a |

CP-1 figures used here (consolidated, US$m): total debt 13,163 and cash 760 at 2026-09-30, liquidity 3,060, LTM Adjusted EBITDA 3,535, total debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA 3.72x, net 3.51x, reported covenant net leverage 3.5x. CP-0 limitations carried: no executed legal documents, no ratings, unexplained Delaware and Texas wording. This handoff corrects neither.
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Sunoco is an Energy Transfer-controlled group of fuel distribution, pipeline, terminal and refinery businesses that scaled quickly through acquisitions. Creditors hold a diversified but acquisition-driven franchise with sponsor-linked governance and open integration risk. | Medium | The partnership agreement, indentures and Offen funding terms are not supplied, so control rights and distribution or borrowing capacity rest on filing summaries. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Fuel Distribution earned 523 US$m of the 1,049 US$m Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026; Refinery earned 238, Pipeline Systems 166 and Terminals 122. | Earnings are broader than a pure distributor, but the refinery is a new, commodity-exposed driver in only its first full year. | High |

| Energy Transfer owns the general partner, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights, and controls SunocoCorp, which appoints the board. | Sponsor control is complete; incentive distributions of 76 US$m in the Q3 2026 distribution take cash before it can reduce debt. | High |

| Parkland, TanQuid and Delta closed between 2025-10-31 and 2026-04-01, and Offen closed on 2026-10-27 for about 600 US$m in cash. | Acquisition appetite is clear; integration, open purchase accounting and Offen funding remain risks to leverage. | High |

| 7-Eleven was about 13% of FY2025 revenues under a 15-year take-or-pay fuel supply agreement that sets minimum annual gross profit. | The minimum gross profit mitigates concentration, but it is the one named customer exposure. | High |

| The Q3 2026 common distribution is 1.0148 US$ per unit, and the Partnership must keep SunocoCorp unit distributions equal through the equalisation period ending 2027-12-31. | Distribution commitments grow with the rate and the unit count, limiting cash retained for debt reduction. | Medium |
### Business and transaction view

The business is a four-segment energy infrastructure and fuel distribution group: Fuel Distribution, Pipeline Systems, Terminals and Refinery. It operates across 33 countries and territories in North America, the Greater Caribbean and Europe, with about 14,000 miles of pipeline, over 170 terminals and capacity to distribute over 17 billion gallons annually (Q3 10-Q page:7). The step change came from the Parkland acquisition on 2025-10-31, which added Canadian and Caribbean distribution and the Burnaby refinery, on top of the NuStar acquisition of 2024-05-03, which added pipelines and terminals. Ownership is concentrated: Energy Transfer owns the general partner, a minority of the common units and all incentive distribution rights, and through SunocoCorp controls the board appointment right. The creditor view is a larger, more diversified earnings base than before the acquisitions, financed largely with debt and preferred equity, under a sponsor whose economic interest (incentive distributions) is separate from that of the debt holders. Documented behaviour since 2024 shows continued acquisition activity paired with reported leverage reduction and rising distributions, which is mixed for creditors rather than adverse. The decisive open items are the fair-value work on Parkland, TanQuid, Delta and Offen, the funding of Offen, and the absence of the executed documents that set distribution, debt and change-of-control limits.
### Company and operating model
| Area | Fact | Category | Source | Credit relevance |

| Business description | Texas master limited partnership engaged in energy infrastructure and fuel distribution; Delaware in the FY2025 10-K and Q1 2026 10-Q wording | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:7; 10-K page:6 | Entity wording changed between filings and is unexplained (see Conflicts) |

| Geography and scale | 33 countries and territories; about 14,000 miles of pipeline; over 170 terminals; about 11,000 branded and partner-branded locations | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:7 | Diversification across regions and fuel supply chains |

| Fuel Distribution | Supplies dealers and distributors, commission agents, company-operated convenience stores and commercial customers; FY2025 network of about 9,200 dealer and distributor sites, about 1,300 commission agent sites, about 330 company-operated sites and over 13,000 commercial customers | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:11 | Contracted volume and brand relationships support volume visibility; margins are per-gallon and narrow |

| Fuel supply | Branded fuel is bought from major oil companies and refiners under agreements of three to five years; largest branded suppliers by volume are Chevron, Exxon, Phillips 66 and Valero | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:12 | Supplier dependence; some purchases come from affiliates of the sponsor (see Ownership) |

| Pipeline Systems | Refined product, crude and ammonia pipelines and 69 terminals, including the J.C. Nolan and ET-S Permian joint ventures | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:21 | Fee-based throughput revenue; Q3 2026 segment Adjusted EBITDA of 166 US$m compared with 182 US$m in Q3 2025 |

| Terminals | Four transmix facilities and 102 refined product terminals (18 in Europe, six in Hawaii, nine in Canada, 20 in the Greater Caribbean and 49 in the continental United States) | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:21 | Storage and throughput fees; the FY2025 10-K counted 83 terminals and excluded TanQuid (10-K page:10 and page:15) |

| Refinery | Burnaby Refinery, British Columbia, operating capacity about 55,000 barrels per day, sold mainly through Sunoco-owned retail in British Columbia, to Vancouver airport and to commercial customers | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:15; Q3 10-Q page:21 | Single-site, commodity-margin exposure; Refinery Adjusted EBITDA was 238 US$m in Q3 2026 |

| Revenue streams | Q3 2026 revenues of 18,029 US$m, of which fuel 17,225, non-fuel 268, lease 47, pipeline throughput 175, terminal throughput 42, refinery 117 and other 155 | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:16 | Revenue is dominated by pass-through fuel sales, so gross profit and Adjusted EBITDA, not revenue, measure scale |

| Segment earnings, Q3 2026 | Fuel Distribution 523, Pipeline Systems 166, Terminals 122, Refinery 238, total 1,049 US$m | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:22 | Fuel Distribution is the largest contributor; the refinery sells largely to other segments (intersegment revenues 853 of 970 US$m) |

| Customer concentration | 7-Eleven, Inc. about 13% of FY2025 total revenues (18% in FY2024); 15-year take-or-pay fuel supply agreement with minimum annual gross profit | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:261 | Named exposure to one distributor; contract supports gross profit |

| Contracted revenue | Remaining performance obligations of 2,038 US$m, of which 123 US$m in the remainder of 2026 and 355 US$m in 2027 | Documentary Fact | Q3 10-Q page:16 | Limited to fixed price and volume contracts, so a small share of total revenue |

| Seasonality | Fuel volumes typically higher in the second and third quarters; commercial volumes higher in winter | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:17 and page:18 | Quarterly results vary; the LTM view smooths this |

| Capital spending | 2026 guidance of 400 to 450 US$m maintenance and at least 600 US$m growth capital expenditure; nine-month accrual-basis capital expenditure of 638 US$m | Management Language (guidance), Documentary Fact (actual) | Q3 10-Q page:44 | Growth spending is discretionary; maintenance is the committed floor |

| Working capital | Moves with crude oil prices and with timing of motor fuel tax, sales tax, interest and rent; fuel inventory mainly on last-in first-out cost | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:18; Q3 10-Q page:11 | Nine-month 2026 working capital inflow of 316 US$m is price- and timing-driven |
| Real estate | 1,861 owned and 2,692 leased sites at 2025-12-31 | Documentary Fact | 10-K page:15 | Lease obligations sit outside the debt figure |

| Management claim: leverage | Release states the Partnership "returns to leverage target in less than one year following the acquisition of Parkland"; the target level is not stated | Management Language | Release Q3 page:2 | Not verifiable from the sources; the reported covenant ratio is 3.5x |
### Company profile
| Attribute | Value | Source |
| Issuer (registrant) | Sunoco LP, Commission File Number 001-35653 | Q3 10-Q page:1 |
| Ticker and exchange | SUN; Texas Stock Exchange in the Q3 2026 10-Q and release; the FY2025 10-K refers to the New York Stock Exchange | Q3 10-Q page:1; 10-K page:2 |
| Legal form and jurisdiction | Texas master limited partnership in the Q2 and Q3 2026 10-Qs; Delaware in the FY2025 10-K and Q1 2026 10-Q | Q3 10-Q page:7; 10-K page:6; Q1 10-Q page:6 |
| Headquarters | 8111 Westchester Drive, Suite 400, Dallas, Texas 75225 | Q3 10-Q page:1 |
| Sector and country (context) | Petroleum Refining; United States | Context file (not issuer evidence) |
| General partner | Sunoco GP LLC, owned 100% by Energy Transfer | Q3 10-Q page:2 and page:7 |
| Controlling holder | Energy Transfer LP: general partner interest, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights; also controls SunocoCorp LLC | Q3 10-Q page:7 |
| Units outstanding at 2026-10-30 | 136,896,738 common units, 16,410,780 Class C units (held by subsidiaries) and 51,517,198 Class D units (held by SunocoCorp) | Q3 10-Q page:1 and page:18 |
| Public common unitholders at 2026-09-30 | 108,432,771 common units | Q3 10-Q page:18 |
| Preferred equity | 1,500,000 Series A Preferred Units, 7.875% fixed-rate reset cumulative perpetual, carried at 1,477 US$m | Q3 10-Q page:3 and page:20 |
| Segments | Fuel Distribution, Pipeline Systems, Terminals, Refinery | Q3 10-Q page:21 |
| Auditor | Grant Thornton LLP, unqualified opinion on FY2025 statements and internal control | 10-K page:217 |
| Fiscal year end | December 31 | 10-K page:1 |
| Credit ratings | Not supplied | Context file (blank) |
| Sponsor | Energy Transfer as controlling holder; no private-equity sponsor is named in the context | Q3 10-Q page:7 |
### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The defining transaction is the Parkland acquisition, completed on 2025-10-31 by Sunoco Retail LLC, a wholly owned corporate subsidiary. Parkland shareholders received 0.295 SunocoCorp units and C$19.80 in cash per Parkland share, or could elect cash or units subject to proration. The Partnership paid about 2.60 billion US$ to Parkland shareholders and transferred 51,517,198 SunocoCorp common units, which it had received in exchange for issuing 51,517,198 Class D Units to SunocoCorp (10-K page:7). Total consideration was 5,015 US$m (4,551 US$m net of cash acquired), against assumed long-term debt of 3,797 US$m, goodwill of 1,528 US$m and intangible assets of 1,871 US$m, all on a preliminary allocation (10-K page:238). The cash portion was funded in part by the September 2025 issuance of 1.00 billion US$ of 5.625% senior notes due 2031 and 900 million US$ of 5.875% senior notes due 2034, and by the 1.5 million Series A Preferred Units sold for net proceeds of about 1.47 billion US$ (10-K page:140). The Parkland senior note exchange closed on 2025-11-07 with about C$1.47 billion and 2.58 billion US$ of Parkland notes tendered, leaving 111 US$m of Parkland notes outstanding at 2025-12-31 (10-K page:140 and page:139); the Q3 10-Q shows those residual Parkland notes redeemed in 2026 (page:14). SunocoCorp was repurposed as a publicly traded corporation holding the Class D Units, and the Partnership must keep SunocoCorp distributions equal to its own through the equalisation period (Q3 10-Q page:19).

In 2026 the Partnership acquired TanQuid on 2026-01-16 (15 fuel terminals in Germany and one in Poland) for 239 US$m with 346 US$m of assumed debt at fair value, funded from cash and the revolving credit facility, and Delta on 2026-04-01 for about 81 US$m, with terminals and distribution assets in five Caribbean markets (Q3 10-Q page:9 and page:10). Purchase accounting for TanQuid is preliminary. After quarter end, on 2026-10-27, Sunoco Retail acquired Offen Petroleum, a US fuel distributor of about 2.5 billion gallons a year, for about 600 US$m in cash plus working capital; the funding source and the effect on 2026-10-31 liquidity are not stated, and fair value work is incomplete (Q3 10-Q page:10). On 2026-10-08 the receivables financing agreement was terminated with no borrowings outstanding (Q3 10-Q page:15).

New debt issued in the period: in March 2025, 1.00 billion US$ of 6.250% senior notes due 2033, used to repay 600 US$m of 5.750% notes due 2025 and part of the revolver (10-K page:140); in September 2025, the 5.625% 2031 and 5.875% 2034 notes above; in March 2026, 600 US$m of 5.375% senior notes due 2031 and 600 US$m of 5.625% senior notes due 2034, both maturing on 2031-07-15 and 2034-07-15, with part of the proceeds used to redeem the 500 US$m 6.000% notes due 2026 and the 600 US$m 6.000% notes due 2027 (Q3 10-Q page:14). Net of these redemptions the March 2026 issuance added 100 US$m of principal. Parkland's remaining notes were redeemed in March 2026, the 3.875% CAD notes due 2026 in June 2026 and the 6.000% CAD notes due 2028 in August 2026. The earlier history includes the NuStar acquisition of 2024-05-03 (about 51.5 million Sunoco common units issued, about 3.5 billion US$ of debt assumed, and NuStar preferred units, subordinated notes and credit facility repaid after closing), the sale of 204 West Texas convenience stores to 7-Eleven on 2024-04-16 for about 1.0 billion US$ with a 586 US$m gain, and the formation of the ET-S Permian joint venture with Energy Transfer on 2024-07-01 (10-K page:240 to page:242).
### Ownership, governance and sponsor behaviour

Energy Transfer owns 100% of the general partner membership interest, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights, and controls SunocoCorp, which owns all Class D Units (Q3 10-Q page:7). Under a Delegation Agreement dated 2025-10-27, Energy Transfer delegated its power to elect, appoint and remove the Sunoco GP LLC board to SunocoCorp; the rights terminate on certain SunocoCorp insolvency events or at Energy Transfer's election, and the general partner agreed not to amend the partnership agreement against those rights or to withdraw while SunocoCorp is listed or not wholly owned by Energy Transfer (10-K page:197). The 10-K states that general partner officers and directors "also have a contractual duty to manage our General Partner in a manner beneficial to Energy Transfer" and that conflicts of interest may arise (10-K page:91). An Omnibus Agreement dated 2025-10-31 has the Partnership indemnify SunocoCorp, provide all general and administrative services and fund SunocoCorp's distributions equal to those on Sunoco common units through the eighth full quarter after closing (10-K page:197 and page:198).
Documented actions, by governance dimension (Python scores these; no score is stated here):
| Dimension | Documented action | Category | Behaviour reading | Source | Evidence quality |

| Control and alignment | Energy Transfer control through the general partner, incentive distribution rights and the delegated board appointment right | Documentary Fact | Neutral or Mixed: control is clear, and incentive distributions at the top tier take 50% of marginal cash, which is a sponsor economic interest separate from creditors | 10-K page:122; Q3 10-Q page:7 | High |

| Distributions | Quarterly common distribution of 1.0148 US$ per unit for Q3 2026, with about 139 US$m to common units, 52 US$m to Class D units and 76 US$m to incentive distribution rights; release calls it the eighth consecutive increase | Documentary Fact; Management Language (the eighth increase and the growth policy); Analyst Interpretation (coverage) | Neutral or Mixed: distributions of 880 US$m paid in nine months 2026 were below operating cash flow of 2,251 US$m in the financial-base handoff, so they were not debt-funded on that comparison | Q3 10-Q page:44; Release Q3 page:3 | High |

| Leverage conduct | Reported covenant net leverage fell from 4.03x at FY2025 to 3.5x at Q3 2026 while the Partnership continued acquiring | Documentary Fact | Supportive on deleveraging; Mixed because Offen is an all-cash purchase whose funding is not stated | 10-K page:251; Q3 10-Q page:15 | High |

| Related-party dealings | Bulk fuel purchases from affiliates of 1,249 US$m in FY2025 and 1,760 US$m in nine months 2026; motor fuel sales to affiliates of 884 US$m in nine months 2026; the general partner is reimbursed for all expenses with no cap | Documentary Fact | Neutral or Mixed: large and growing affiliate flows without a stated pricing test | 10-K page:256; Q3 10-Q page:16 | High |

| Financing structure | Series A preferred equity of 1.5 billion US$ sold in 2025; Class D units issued to SunocoCorp for Parkland consideration rather than debt | Documentary Fact | Supportive: part of the Parkland price was met with equity-like units, not debt | 10-K page:7 and page:140 | High |

| Creditor-adverse actions | No priming, uptiering, drop-down, non-pro-rata exchange or collateral release is described in the sources. The Parkland note exchange was a private exchange offer for Parkland noteholders. | Insufficient Information on indenture capacity | Not assessable for legal capacity, since indentures are not supplied | 10-K page:140 | Insufficient |

Legal capacity, willingness and feasibility stay separate. Capacity: the partnership agreement and indentures are not supplied, so limits on restricted payments, debt incurrence and change of control are not assessed; the GoZone bonds carry a 101% repurchase right after a change of control followed by a ratings decline within 60 days (Q3 10-Q page:15). Willingness: distributions have risen every quarter per the release, and acquisitions have continued. Feasibility: liquidity of 3,060 US$m and reported leverage of 3.5x at 2026-09-30 per the financial-base handoff support near-term capacity.
### Timeline
| Date | Event | Type | Source |
| 2024-03-13 | Zenith European terminals (Amsterdam, Bantry Bay) acquired for 185 US$m | Acquisition | 10-K page:241 |
| 2024-04-16 | 204 West Texas convenience stores sold to 7-Eleven for about 1.0 billion US$ | Disposal | 10-K page:242 |

| 2025-10-31 | Parkland acquisition closed; Omnibus Agreement signed | Acquisition | 10-K page:7; page:197 |
| 2025-11-07 | Parkland note exchange offer closed | Refinancing | 10-K page:140 |
| 2026-01-16 | TanQuid acquisition closed | Acquisition | Q3 10-Q page:9 |
| 2026-03 | 5.375% 2031 and 5.625% 2034 notes issued; 2026 and 2027 6.000% notes redeemed | Refinancing | Q3 10-Q page:14 |
| 2026-04-01 | Delta acquisition closed | Acquisition | Q3 10-Q page:10 |
| 2026-10-08 (subsequent event) | Receivables financing agreement terminated | Subsequent event | Q3 10-Q page:15 |
| 2026-10-22 (subsequent event) | Q3 2026 distribution announced | Subsequent event | Q3 10-Q page:44 |
| 2026-10-27 (subsequent event) | Offen Petroleum acquired for about 600 US$m | Subsequent event | Q3 10-Q page:10 |
### Conflicts logged
| Topic | Span one | Span two | Effect |

| Jurisdiction and exchange | "We are a Delaware master limited partnership." (10-K page:6) | "We are a Texas master limited partnership." (Q3 10-Q page:7) | Logged, not reconciled. The 10-K auditor opinion also reads "Sunoco LP (a Delaware limited partnership)" (10-K page:217). The cause and date of any change are not stated; issuer and guarantor entity naming needs caution |

| Adjusted EBITDA headline | "Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $1.060 billion, excluding one-time transaction-related expenses(2)" (Release Q3 page:2) | "Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 was $1.049 billion" (Release Q3 page:2) | Both in the same release. The release says the 1,049 US$m figure included 11 US$m of one-time transaction-related expenses; the filing figure of 1,049 US$m is used |
### Credit translations

Evidence: Energy Transfer holds the general partner, the incentive distribution rights and the delegated board appointment right (10-K page:197, Q3 10-Q page:7). Risk mechanic: control and the top-tier incentive share (50% of marginal cash above the highest target, 10-K page:122) mean the controlling party benefits from distribution growth while creditors benefit from retained cash. Credit implication: monitoring posture should weight distribution policy and any change in control provisions; the debt documents that govern restricted payments are not supplied.

Evidence: Four acquisitions closed in twelve months with open fair value work (10-K page:238; Q3 10-Q page:9 and page:10). Risk mechanic: acquired earnings enter the trailing base gradually while acquired debt and purchase prices enter the balance sheet at once, so leverage ratios and goodwill can move with the accounting allocation. Credit implication: refinancing and leverage tolerance depend on integration delivering the earnings behind the CP-1 trailing ratio of 3.72x; the Offen funding and the CP-1 liquidity of 3,060 US$m should be read together.

Evidence: 7-Eleven accounted for about 13% of FY2025 revenues under a take-or-pay supply agreement (10-K page:261). Risk mechanic: a single customer with a contractual minimum gross profit stabilises Fuel Distribution earnings but concentrates counterparty risk. Credit implication: revenue durability is supported at the segment level, and a loss or renegotiation of the contract is a named downside to monitor.

Evidence: The refinery's output is sold largely to other segments (Q3 10-Q page:22). Risk mechanic: Refinery segment earnings depend on crude differentials and intersegment transfer terms that the sources do not describe. Credit implication: margin and cash-flow risk from a single-site asset is a key uncertainty; the transfer pricing basis is not supplied.
### Consumer readiness
| Consumer | Readiness | What to take from this handoff | Why it matters | Gap and action |

| CP-2 | Ready with limitations | Segment earnings, customer concentration, acquisition timeline, new notes issued | Operating drivers and perimeter changes bear on the earnings and liquidity assessment | Offen funding and pro forma earnings are not supplied; flag trailing-period comparability |

| CP-5 | Ready with limitations | Conflicts, governance table, related-party flows, management claims tagged as such | Evidence review needs the ownership, control and management-language boundaries | Indentures and partnership agreement are not supplied; treat creditor-protection capacity as not assessed |
## Calculations
| Calculation | Inputs | Result |
| Segment earnings sum, Q3 2026 | 523 + 166 + 122 + 238 (Q3 10-Q page:22) | 1,049, equals consolidated Adjusted EBITDA |
| Revenue mix check, Q3 2026 | 17,225 + 268 + 47 + 175 + 42 + 117 + 155 (Q3 10-Q page:16) | 18,029, equals total revenues |
| Net principal change, March 2026 notes | Issued 600 + 600 less redeemed 500 + 600 (Q3 10-Q page:14) | 100 added |
| Distribution to common, Class D and incentive holders, Q3 2026 | 139 + 52 + 76 (Q3 10-Q page:44) | 267, approximate and rounded in the source |
| Dismissed: shares of earnings | No segment share percentages are stated, to keep every figure traceable | Not calculated |
## Gaps
| Gap | Detail | Severity | Action |

| Partnership agreement and indentures not supplied | Restricted payment, debt incurrence, change of control and guarantor release terms cannot be read | Material | Obtain the executed documents before any capacity conclusion |

| Offen funding and effect on leverage not stated | About 600 US$m cash purchase after quarter end | Material | Use the next filing for funding disclosure; treat post-quarter leverage as not assessed |
| Purchase accounting open | Parkland, TanQuid, Delta and Offen allocations are preliminary or not yet determined | Moderate | Watch for goodwill and deferred tax adjustments |
| Jurisdiction and exchange change unexplained | See Conflicts logged | Moderate | Confirm entity naming in debt documents |
| Refinery transfer pricing and unit economics not described | Refinery sells mainly to other segments | Moderate | Request segment transfer terms |
| Leverage target not stated | The release cites a "leverage target" without a level | Minor | Treat as management language |
| Ratings and sponsor support commitments not supplied | No rating or support agreement in the sources | Moderate | Not assessed |
## Next module

CP-2 should use the segment earnings, the acquisition timeline and the Offen subsequent event from this handoff with the CP-1 liquidity and maturity data, and should flag Offen funding and pro forma earnings as open. CP-5 should treat the conflicts table, the management-language items and the unsupplied legal documents as evidence limits and trace the governance rows to their citations.

This module gives the fundamental credit view of Sunoco LP as of 2026-11-05 under the credit_snapshot pathway. It synthesises the accepted source-readiness, financial-base and business-context handoffs for the consolidated Partnership, in USD millions, for Q3 2026 and FY2025. It gives no peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Sunoco LP's credit profile has improved to 3.51x net leverage and USD 3,060 million of liquidity, supported by diversified earnings, but it rests on recently acquired earnings, management-adjusted EBITDA and sponsor control. | Medium | Trailing earnings are not pro forma, debt documents are not supplied, and the funding of the Offen acquisition is not stated. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Net debt is 3.51x trailing Adjusted EBITDA at Q3 2026, down from 6.11x at FY2025, with covenant net leverage reported at 3.5x. | Reported headroom to the 5.50x ceiling is wide, but part of the fall reflects acquired earnings entering the trailing base. | Medium |

| Liquidity is USD 3,060 million against USD 1,049 million of notes due in 2027 and USD 2,723 million due in 2029. | Near-term maturities are well covered; the 2027 notes still depend on market access for refinancing. | High |

| Trailing Adjusted EBITDA covers cash interest of USD 726 million 4.87 times, and operating cash flow of USD 2,251 million exceeded distributions of USD 880 million in nine months 2026. | Debt service is comfortable on a cash basis, though working capital added USD 316 million to operating cash flow. | Medium |

| Energy Transfer controls the general partner, incentive distributions of USD 76 million were declared for Q3 2026, and the Offen purchase of about USD 600 million closed after quarter end. | Sponsor economics and acquisitions can slow deleveraging; the debt documents that limit distributions are not supplied. | Medium |
### Credit view

Sunoco LP is a sponsor-controlled fuel distribution and midstream credit whose leverage has fallen to about 3.5x and whose liquidity is ample. Its strongest support is scale and diversification: trailing Adjusted EBITDA of USD 3,535 million across four segments, net debt of 3.51x that figure, and liquidity of USD 3,060 million against USD 1,049 million of notes due in 2027. The weakest point is that the improvement rests on recently acquired earnings, management-adjusted EBITDA and a sponsor whose incentive distributions and board control sit beside creditor interests, while funding for the USD 600 million Offen purchase is not described. Whether Parkland integration and refinery margins keep earnings at this level decides whether leverage keeps falling.
### Key findings

Leverage has fallen sharply, but part of the fall is perimeter change. Sunoco LP's net debt over trailing Adjusted EBITDA fell from 6.11x at FY2025 to 3.51x at Q3 2026, and the reported covenant net leverage fell from 4.03x to 3.5x [CP-1]. The mechanism is that Parkland (acquired on 2025-10-31) contributed two months to FY2025 earnings but eleven months to the Q3 2026 trailing window while its debt was fully on the balance sheet at both dates [CP-1, CP-1A]. The implication is that headroom against the 5.50x covenant ceiling is wide on the reported basis, yet the trajectory should be judged on pro forma earnings that the sources do not supply.

Liquidity is strong against a staggered maturity profile. Sunoco LP held USD 760 million of cash and USD 2,300 million of undrawn revolver, total USD 3,060 million, at 2026-09-30, after USD 111 million drawn and USD 84 million of letters of credit [CP-1]. Maturities are USD 1,049 million in 2027, USD 900 million in 2028, USD 2,723 million in 2029 and USD 2,309 million in 2030 including the revolver [CP-1]. The 2027 notes are classified as long-term only on management's intent and ability to refinance, so the mechanism is market access rather than cash on hand. The implication is that refinancing risk is low in the next twelve months and moderate in 2027 to 2029, when USD 4,672 million falls due.

Debt service is well covered on a cash basis. Trailing Adjusted EBITDA of USD 3,535 million covers trailing cash interest of USD 726 million 4.87 times, against a covenant minimum of 2.25x that the filings do not report a figure against [CP-1]. Only USD 398 million of debt is variable-rate, so a 100 basis point rate move changes annual interest expense by about USD 4 million (Q3 10-Q page:48). The implication is limited interest-rate sensitivity; the more relevant sensitivity is operating, not financial.

Cash generation covers distributions, with timing help. Nine-month 2026 operating cash flow of USD 2,251 million exceeded capital expenditure of USD 579 million and distributions of USD 880 million [CP-1]. The mechanism includes a USD 316 million working-capital inflow, a USD 102 million last-in first-out liquidation benefit to pre-tax income and a USD 94 million non-cash foreign exchange loss [CP-1]. Distribution commitments rise with the rate and unit count and include equal payments to SunocoCorp through 2027-12-31 and USD 76 million of incentive distributions for Q3 2026 [CP-1A]. The implication is that free cash flow after distributions is positive (see Calculations) but is not a stable annuity: it depends on working capital timing and fuel prices.

Earnings quality needs care. Adjusted EBITDA is a management measure that adds back USD 200 million of unconsolidated affiliate EBITDA, USD 131 million of other non-cash adjustments and removes a USD 445 million favourable inventory valuation adjustment in nine months 2026 [CP-1]. Covenant ratios use credit-agreement definitions that are not supplied [CP-0, CP-1]. The implication is that the derived ratios in this synthesis are a guide and the covenant headroom is a reported claim, not a verified result.

Structure and control weigh on creditor protection. Energy Transfer owns the general partner, 28,463,967 common units and all incentive distribution rights, and controls the board appointment right through SunocoCorp [CP-1A]. Notes are guaranteed by subsidiaries and rank effectively behind secured obligations including the revolver, and structurally behind debt of non-guarantor subsidiaries, which hold USD 11.73 billion of long-term assets (Q3 10-Q page:47); the line for lease-related financing and other subsidiary debt is USD 597 million and its obligors are not identified [CP-1]. The implication is that the capacity to pay out cash or add debt depends on indenture and partnership agreement terms that are not supplied, so legal capacity is not assessed.

Acquisition pace is the main forward risk. Four acquisitions closed within twelve months, the latest being Offen on 2026-10-27 for about USD 600 million in cash [CP-1A]. The mechanism is that purchase prices and acquired debt enter the balance sheet at once while earnings arrive gradually, and fair value work is open. An all-debt illustration would lift net leverage to about 3.68x before any Offen earnings (see Calculations). The implication is that further leverage movement depends on funding choice and integration.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. Scale and diversification (Documentary Fact): four segments with Fuel Distribution, Pipeline Systems, Terminals and Refinery all contributing in Q3 2026, and operations in 33 countries and territories [CP-1A]. This reduces dependence on one margin source and supports revenue visibility. Fee-based and contracted income (Documentary Fact): pipeline and terminal throughput, remaining performance obligations of USD 2,038 million and a 15-year take-or-pay fuel supply agreement with minimum gross profit with the largest customer [CP-1A]. This supports cash conversion in weaker fuel-margin periods. Liquidity and maturity management (Documentary Fact): USD 3,060 million of liquidity, a revolver maturing 2030-06-17 and 2026 and 2027 notes replaced by notes due 2031 and 2034 [CP-1, CP-1A]. This lowers near-term refinancing risk. Deleveraging record (Documentary Fact): covenant net leverage reported at 4.03x, 3.98x, 3.7x and 3.5x across the last four reporting dates [CP-1]. This shows a funding and earnings path that creditors can monitor. Equity cushion (Analyst Interpretation): total equity of USD 8,512 million including USD 1,477 million of preferred units sits beneath USD 13,163 million of debt, which is 60.7% of debt plus equity (see Calculations) [CP-1]. Preferred and Class D equity were used for part of the Parkland price [CP-1A].

Weaknesses. Acquisition dependence (Documentary Fact): Parkland, TanQuid, Delta and Offen in twelve months with open fair value work [CP-1A]. This makes trailing metrics unrepresentative and exposes leverage to integration. Sponsor control and cash leakage (Documentary Fact): Energy Transfer control, incentive distributions at the top tier share and a general partner that must favour Energy Transfer's interests under its contractual duty [CP-1A]. This competes with debt reduction for cash. Commodity and single-site exposure (Analyst Interpretation): the Burnaby Refinery earned USD 238 million of Segment Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026, largely on intersegment sales whose pricing terms are not described [CP-1A]. This adds margin volatility. Thin per-gallon margins and working capital swings (Analyst Interpretation): fuel is most of revenue and working capital moved by USD 316 million in nine months 2026 [CP-1, CP-1A]. Customer concentration (Documentary Fact): 7-Eleven was about 13% of FY2025 revenues [CP-1A]. Disclosure limits (Insufficient Information): the indentures, credit agreement, partnership agreement, ratings and pro forma earnings are not supplied, which stops conclusions on covenant headroom, restricted payments and rating-linked pricing. Market view of the debt (Documentary Fact): the aggregate fair value of debt was USD 12.88 billion against a carrying amount of USD 13.16 billion at 2026-09-30, the reverse of the position at 2025-12-31 (Q3 10-Q page:15); the sources do not explain the move.
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Acquisition integration and funding | Purchase prices and acquired debt arrive before earnings; Offen funding not stated | Leverage could stall above the current level; refinancing needs rise | Material |

| Sponsor control and distributions | Incentive distributions and equalisation payments take cash; board appointed through SunocoCorp | Slower deleveraging; creditor protections depend on documents not supplied | Material |
| Fuel margin and working capital volatility | Per-gallon margins and crude price swings drive earnings and cash timing | Cash conversion and liquidity can swing between quarters | Material |
| Refinery and intersegment dependence | Refinery sells largely to other segments at undisclosed transfer terms | Segment earnings may not be transferable evidence of external margin | Material |
| 2027 to 2029 refinancing wall | Notes due in 2027 are classed long-term only on refinancing intent | Market access determines cost and timing | Minor |
| Definition and perimeter risk | Management Adjusted EBITDA, covenant definitions and partial-period acquisitions | Headroom claims cannot be verified | Material |

All inputs are USD millions from the handoffs unless a page is cited.

## Gaps
| Gap | Why it matters | Affects | Severity | Action |

| Debt documents and partnership agreement not supplied | Restricted payments, debt incurrence, change of control and guarantor release limits are unknown | Creditor protection, covenant headroom | Material | Obtain executed documents; until then treat legal capacity as not assessed |
| No pro forma earnings for acquisitions | Trailing leverage mixes partial and full periods | Leverage trajectory | Material | Use pro forma disclosure when available; label ratios as derived |
| Offen funding not stated | Post-quarter leverage and liquidity cannot be updated | Liquidity, leverage | Material | Read the next filing for funding |
| Ratings and market data not supplied | Rating-linked pricing step-down and market view cannot be tested | Refinancing assessment | Moderate | Not assessed |
| Business-context readiness for this synthesis was "ready with limitations" | Confidence capped below High | Whole synthesis | Moderate | Carry the limitations of the earlier handoffs |
| Refinery transfer pricing not described | Segment profit may not reflect external margin | Earnings quality | Moderate | Request segment transfer terms |
| Covenant interest coverage figure not printed | Headroom against the 2.25x minimum cannot be shown | Covenant headroom | Moderate | Obtain compliance certificate if available |
## Next module

CP-5 should test the leverage, liquidity, maturity and governance statements here against the filing pages cited in the earlier handoffs, with attention to the derived ratios, the management-language items and the unsupplied legal documents. The first evidence action is to obtain the credit agreement, indentures and partnership agreement.
